primary_sources: Stanford Applied Statistics & Hypothesis Testing Guidelines

rules.rule_name: Formulation of Null and Alternative Hypotheses
rules.explanation: Testing data without clear prior null (H0) and alternative (H1) hypotheses leads to p-hacking and false discovery rates.
rules.do: Explicitly state H0 and H1, choose the significance level (alpha = 0.05) beforehand, and verify underlying distributional assumptions (normality, homoscedasticity).
rules.dont: Do not run multiple uncalibrated statistical tests post-hoc to hunt for significant p-values.

rules.rule_name: Appropriate Test Selection Based on Data Distribution
rules.explanation: Applying parametric tests (e.g., Student t-test) on heavily skewed or non-normal distributions distorts Type I error rates.
rules.do: Check parametric assumptions (e.g., Shapiro-Wilk test) and use non-parametric alternatives (e.g., Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon) when assumptions fail.
rules.dont: Do not blindly apply parametric t-tests or ANOVA without testing for normality and equal variances.

rules.rule_name: Sample Size Calculation and Power Analysis
rules.explanation: Underpowered experiments fail to detect real effects, while overly large samples make trivial differences statistically significant without practical importance.
rules.do: Perform power analysis to compute required sample size based on Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE), statistical power (1-beta = 0.8), and significance level.
rules.dont: Do not terminate A/B tests early or evaluate experiments without calculating required statistical power.

rules.rule_name: Confidence Interval Reporting and Effect Size
rules.explanation: P-values only indicate if an effect exists, not how large or practically meaningful the effect is in real-world applications.
rules.do: Report effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d, Cramer's V) alongside 95% Confidence Intervals for all statistical outcomes.
rules.dont: Do not report p-values alone without accompanying effect sizes and confidence intervals.
